title: Workshop: Open Source Agent Investigations: Security Arena, Distilled Traces, and Auto Optimization

segments.text: DEVINA JAIN: Hi, my name is Devina.
I work as a researcher at Lamda.
I work on model evaluations and safety.
I basically come from a physical AI and self-driving background,
so I did evaluations and safety there as well.
I'm going to make a few analogies to that,
which is why I call that out.
Today, I'm going to talk about a month-long security competition
that we conducted with the help of Berkeley RTI.
Basically, we had teams compete as attackers and defenders
on a leaderboard and compete against each other
on prompt injection challenges.
We're going to talk about how that went, what we found out.
So why are we interested in prompt injection?
Let's talk about echo leak, because that's
of production incident that we want
to be able to catch before it happens.
So what happened here was an attacker sent an email
to someone's inbox.
This person didn't do anything, they
didn't interact with the email.
They just asked Copilot a question.
Copilot read this email, read its embedded instructions, which
were harmful, complied with it, and exfiltrated
their entire inbox.
This is the thing that we want to be
able to catch with testing, and it is also really difficult
to solve, because the root cause is architectural.
LLMs process instructions and data in the same channel,
and they can't tell when they are
getting an instruction that's wrong
or ingesting data that's incorrect.

The first half is going to focus on the competition.

a good realistic scenario?
How do you know that you're not just measuring noise?

to measure what makes a scenario meaningful.
The first thing is a scenario should be difficult.

they should have maybe a 50% balanced win rate.
This scenario should be sensitive.
So if you run a strong model against a weak model,
it should actually be able to distinguish
between the capabilities.
And third, you want it to be--
you want this scenario to not just be broken in one round,
